content:
**Quick answer:** There is no universal list of foods everyone with arthritis must avoid. For general health, it is sensible to limit foods high in saturated fat, salt and free sugars, while avoiding unnecessary elimination diets. If a particular food repeatedly seems to affect your symptoms, discuss it with a GP or dietitian before making major restrictions.

## The most important thing to know first

If you are searching for foods to avoid with arthritis, the honest starting point is that there is no universal list of foods everyone with arthritis needs to cut out, and restrictive arthritis diets are usually unnecessary.

Arthritis describes many different conditions. Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and gout do not all have the same causes or treatment, and no single food has been proven to worsen every type of arthritis in every person. Individual experience is worth noticing, but it does not justify removing entire food groups for everyone.

> **"Eat less often" is different from "never eat"**
>
> UK healthy-eating guidance supports having foods high in saturated fat, free sugars and salt less often and in smaller amounts. These foods are not automatically arthritis triggers, and a balanced diet can include flexibility and enjoyment.

## Worth eating less often, for general health

Foods high in saturated fat: fatty cuts of meat, sausages, bacon, butter, lard, cream, some cheeses, cakes, biscuits, pastries, chocolate and foods containing significant amounts of coconut or palm oil. The NHS advises reducing saturated fat because too much can raise blood cholesterol and increase the risk of heart disease, not because it directly causes every arthritis flare. Alternatives can include olive or rapeseed oil, oily fish, nuts, seeds, avocado, leaner meat, beans and lentils.

Foods high in free sugars: sugary drinks, biscuits, doughnuts and similar foods are best treated as less-frequent choices. Claims that "sugar causes arthritis" are too simplistic, and whole fruit is not the same thing: it provides fibre, vitamins and minerals alongside naturally occurring sugars.

Salty foods: processed meats, some ready meals, takeaways, salty snacks, sauces, stock cubes, some canned foods, cured fish and some cheeses. Much of the salt people eat is already inside packaged food rather than added at the table, so comparing labels helps. Too much salt can raise blood pressure.

Some ultra-processed foods contain large amounts of saturated fat, salt or sugar, but processed does not automatically mean unhealthy. Frozen vegetables, canned beans and wholemeal sliced bread fit comfortably into a balanced diet. Rather than deciding whether every food is "processed enough" to avoid, check what it actually contains.

## The foods people ask about most

Tomatoes, potatoes and other nightshades: there is no general NHS recommendation for people with arthritis to avoid them. Boiled or baked potatoes with their skins are a reasonable choice; the "less often" versions are deep-fried chips, heavily salted chips and processed potato snacks.

Dairy: no general recommendation to avoid it. Milk, yoghurt and cheese provide protein and calcium. If you have a diagnosed allergy, intolerance or another medical reason to avoid dairy, that is different, and you should make sure you have suitable alternatives.

Gluten: most people with arthritis do not need a gluten-free diet. Gluten must be avoided by people with conditions such as coeliac disease, but that is separate from general arthritis dietary advice. If you think wheat or gluten repeatedly causes symptoms, speak to your GP or a registered dietitian before starting a strict exclusion diet.

Citrus fruit: no arthritis recommendation requires avoiding oranges, lemons and other citrus fruits unless you have an allergy, intolerance, medicine interaction or another individual reason.

Coffee: not universally prohibited. Caffeine may affect sleep in some people, and poor sleep makes living with pain harder, so adjust your intake if caffeine affects your sleep or you have been advised to limit it.

Red and processed meat: processed meats such as bacon, sausages, salami and chorizo can be high in salt and saturated fat, but red meat itself does not have to be eliminated. Consider portion size, frequency, leaner cuts and how it is cooked, and replace some meat-based meals with beans, lentils or fish if those suit you.

Alcohol: this one needs particular care because it can interact with medicines and may be unsuitable with some medical conditions. If you take arthritis medication, ask your pharmacist, GP or rheumatology team whether alcohol is safe for you rather than relying on general internet advice. Do not stop or change prescribed medication to accommodate alcohol.

Gout: gout needs separate consideration from general arthritis diet advice. If you have gout or think particular foods or drinks trigger attacks, speak to your GP or another healthcare professional involved in your care.

## Should you try an elimination diet?

Be cautious. Removing multiple foods at once can make your diet nutritionally unbalanced, make it impossible to know which change mattered, make eating unnecessarily stressful and remove nutritious foods without good reason.

A better approach is a simple food and symptom diary before making major restrictions: record what you ate, when, what symptoms followed, whether the same thing happens repeatedly, and other possible factors such as activity, sleep, illness or stress. Arthritis symptoms naturally fluctuate, so one painful day after eating a particular food does not prove the food caused it.

## Use traffic-light labels to compare, not to ban

Many packaged UK foods use red, amber and green traffic-light labels. Rather than treating red as forbidden, use the colours to compare similar products and think about how often and how much you eat them. Front-of-pack information is particularly useful for comparing saturated fat, sugars and salt.

## What to eat instead

A balanced eating pattern matters more than a long list of banned foods: vegetables, fruit, higher-fibre starchy carbohydrates, beans and pulses, fish, eggs and other protein foods, dairy or suitable alternatives, and small amounts of unsaturated oils and spreads. For rheumatoid arthritis, Mediterranean-style eating is often discussed as a healthy pattern.

Simple swaps that do not feel restrictive: water or lower-sugar drinks instead of sugary fizzy drinks; fruit or unsalted nuts instead of salty snacks; fish, leaner meat, beans or lentils instead of fatty processed meat; higher-fibre or wholegrain cereals instead of refined ones; small amounts of unsaturated oils instead of butter or lard for everything; baked, grilled, steamed or poached meals instead of deep-fried ones.

These are options, not rules. Your diet should reflect your preferences, culture, budget, medical needs and ability to shop and prepare food.

> **Diet cannot cure arthritis**
>
> There is no diet proven to cure arthritis, and this matters most for inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis. Do not stop or reduce prescribed arthritis medication because you have changed what you eat.

## Key takeaways

- There is no universal list of foods everyone with arthritis must avoid.
- Foods high in saturated fat, salt and free sugars are generally better eaten less often, not banned.
- There is no general recommendation to avoid tomatoes, potatoes, dairy or gluten simply because you have arthritis.
- One difficult day does not prove a particular food caused your symptoms; a food and symptom diary can reveal repeated patterns.
- Diet does not cure arthritis or replace medical treatment.

## Frequently asked questions

### What are the main foods to avoid with arthritis?

There is no universal list. For general health, it is sensible to eat foods high in saturated fat, salt and free sugars less often and in smaller amounts rather than banning specific foods because of arthritis.

### Is dairy bad for arthritis?

Dairy does not need to be avoided simply because you have arthritis. If you have an allergy, intolerance or another medical reason to avoid it, ask a healthcare professional or dietitian about suitable alternatives.

### Is gluten bad for arthritis?

Most people with arthritis do not need to avoid gluten. A gluten-free diet is necessary for conditions such as coeliac disease but is not a general arthritis treatment.

### Can certain foods trigger rheumatoid arthritis symptoms?

Some people report that particular foods appear to worsen symptoms, but there is no strong evidence that one specific dietary change improves rheumatoid arthritis for everyone.

## A gentle next step

Searching for foods to avoid can quickly lead to long lists of supposedly inflammatory foods that make eating more confusing and restrictive than it needs to be. A more practical approach is a varied diet, nutritious foods most of the time, and attention to your own consistent patterns without blaming every flare on food. If you believe a particular food repeatedly affects your symptoms, or you are considering removing an entire food group, speak to your GP or a registered dietitian. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
